body.heading: Straight from your account
paragraphs: When you pay with a debit card, the money leaves your bank account, usually within a day or two. There is no bill at the end of the month and no interest, because it was your money all along.
That direct link is the card's strength and its risk. A mistaken or fraudulent payment affects your real balance straight away, which is why glancing at your transactions regularly matters.

body.heading: Small habits that protect you
paragraphs: Your PIN is the key to the card: never share it, and shield the keypad when you type it. Banks do not ask for your PIN by phone, text, or email — anyone who does is trying to trick you.
Turn on transaction alerts if your bank offers them. A quick buzz for each payment means a charge you do not recognise gets spotted in minutes rather than at the end of the month.

body.heading: Watch the balance, not just the card
paragraphs: Because payments can take a day to settle, the balance on screen may not show everything you have already spent. Keeping a small cushion in the account — even $20 or $30 — protects you from accidental overdrafts and the fees that can follow.

If you share the account with anyone, agree that both of you check before large purchases. Most debit card surprises in shared accounts are communication gaps, not carelessness — and a ten-second check prevents nearly all of them.

takeaway: A debit card spends your own money directly, so guard the PIN, switch on alerts, and keep a small cushion in the account.
